etymology.text: From the Latin tolerare, meaning ‘to bear, to put up with’.

story.text: “Aye, but there’s this in it, Dowlas,” said the landlord, speaking in a tone of much candour and tolerance.

etymology.text: From the Latin tolerare, meaning ‘to bear, to put up with’.

story.text: It was nothing to her that the kindness took the form of tolerant patronage; she was used to that.

etymology.text: From the Old English twelfta, meaning ‘twelfth’.

story.text: When the twelfth day after the accident came, I was taken to the sale, a few miles out of London.

etymology.text: From the Latin varius, meaning ‘changing, spotted’.

story.text: Mr. Snagsby, as a timid man, is accustomed to cough with a variety of expressions, and so to save words.

etymology.text: From the Latin vegetare, meaning ‘to enliven’.

story.text: In the end, wisely and carefully we shall readjust the balance of animal and vegetable life to suit our human needs.
story.source: H. G. Wells, The Time Machine, 1895

etymology.text: From the Latin vehiculum, meaning ‘carrier’.

story.text: As he walked briskly along the road, he heard behind him, the noise of some vehicle, approaching at a furious pace.

etymology.text: Made in English from wide + eyed: with eyes wide open.

story.text: Louisa, Mrs. Vincy’s darling, now ran to her with wide-eyed serious excitement...

etymology.text: From the Dutch jacht, meaning ‘a hunting ship’.

story.text: I must not forget that we went on board the yacht, where they all three descended into the cabin, and were busy with some papers.
